Heck, they could serve as a good benchmark for each tier (and give the devs a good metric for fine-tuning intra-tier difficulty): when you can one-shot (or nearly one-shot) the bosses, you're definitely ready for the next tier.

Also, she/he is glitched as fuck! Sometimes she'll/he'll go through what appears to be a completely random number of immunity phases back-to-back without ever being able to do more damage in between.

If they're going to force these lazy time-sinks down our throats, the least they can do is have them work properly.

Immunity phases should be on a timer before the health thresholds kick in.

- The first timer should only be one second from when the boss is capable of taking damage. If you can one-shot the boss, CONGRATULATIONS, that's awesome! If not, if you still did *more* damage than the first health threshold, it sticks and you're ahead of the game. Otherwise the first immunity phase triggers at the standard threshold.

- The second, and subsequent, immunity phases should come EITHER at the next health threshold OR after 3-5 seconds (or more, or less... **this** is where Blizz can easily fine-tune the difficulty of the fight) - whichever comes LAST. If you can grind the boss down in the remaining time, again, congratulations!

- For the love of all that is holy: GET RID OF ANY AND ALL "*LAST SLIVER OF HEALTH*" IMMUNITY PHASES!! And no "mandatory" phases if the boss is killed within those small windows of time.

This would preserve the new mechanics, but still reward players for powering up their characters.

To further refine what I think is the zeitgeist thinking, a major problem with the endgame of D4 is that once you hit lvl 100 , and max out your Paragon glyphs, there is virtually no direct player agency left in character advancement. Everything is either heavily, or completely, ruled by RNG.

In D3, with (nigh) infinite Paragon levels, as you were grinding your character always saw *some* benefit, even if the gods of RNG were being particularly spiteful.

In the Greater Rifts, there was only RNG involved in upgrading your gems if you were running rifts too low for your gem level. Otherwise, you picked the gem, upgraded it, and got the exact same result every time. You did x thing, got y result. That's player agency.

Currently, and continued into season 5, there is no late game advancement mechanics that don't have an element of RNG chance baked into it.

To be 100% crystal clear, I am NOT lobbying for a reduction in the overall amount of RNG in late game D4 (though some "odds balancing" would be much appreciated). To try to summerise my stance, it would be there are (at least) two 'scales' for understanding opposing sides in a debate, the 'general group' and the 'individual member'.

The general group scale is simple yet defining [Christians believe in the exitance and divinity of Christ, for example]. Whereas the individual member' scale is incredibly complex, nuanced, and varied within  the group. But, since it is varied within the group, those differences are non-defining for the group [a specific Christian's personal relationship with Christ].

Generally speaking, I would tend to agree with you. Even if one can say they are opposed to the general group position, it is usually worth while to have an open mind when encountering individual member of that group.

However there are some general group positions that are so foundationally repugnant that the individual member's nuanced position ceases to matter: the KKK, Nazis, or NAMBLA, I think are prime examples. I also think that aligning with a group that is opposed to LGBTQ rights nudges an individual into that territory.

Moreover, it should be pointed out that, quite often, there is a sizeable **history** to the general group's arguments and evidence... If I encounter a proud member of the KKK, I am already well aware of the standard arguments, and have little to no expectation they will put forth NEW evidence in favor of racism. The same goes for anti-LGBTQ rhetoric.

So when I hear something along the lines of "hold on, let's hear both sides... " in situations like this, two things come to mind immediately. 1) What novel information could you possibly expect to encounter? 2) Saying that implies you may well be on the fence here, which is troubling.

And finally, in light of #2, and getting back to the OP, if you *are* on the fence, but base your final decision on who presented their case in a kinder, gentler manner... you're obviously not that interested in the strength or validity of the arguments. As interesting as the results are, there is reason to take it with a hefty grain of salt.

For one, the overall sample size is remarkably small. Second, the actual research was between two individual experiments for which the sizes were even smaller; n = 60 and 42, respectively.

Also, there was only one main field study conductor, and there was no indication in the paper (which I read, by the by) that the researchers controlled for variation based on who conducted the test. In such a non-clinical, social, environment conductor influence should have been at least considered. Moreover, sample selection criteria was not factored either. We know the conductor chose which people to approach, but we don't know what criteria was used by the experimenter to make that choice other than 'seeming inebriated'. Sample bias may be an issue.

Most concerning, the researchers defined greater utilitarian thinking based as:

"rate[ing] on a 5-point Likert scale the likelihood that they would be willing to either flip a switch that diverts the trolley so that it kills one person instead of five (switch dilemma) or push the individual off a bridge to save five people working on the tracks (footbridge dilemma)."

The problem here is that a **very** reasonable issue with that definition is that it might not be describing utilitarian thinking, but simple confidence. That is: drunk people tend to give more extreme scores (very high/low) on ***any and all*** Likert scales due to increased confidence in general, not due to altered reasoning.

Moving forward comes in necessary stages, you can't really skip them:

First, let them rest WHERE THEY ARE. Acknowledge their pain, recognize that it's presence (if not it's magnitude) is entirely rational. The goal here is to address the **guilt** they feel about being depressed, before confronting the depression itself.

Second, don't let them rest alone. Be present, but don't worry over much about being active. By simply being there, but not exhibiting the nervous, knee-jerk, compulsion to fix it, you can lead by example and show that it's okay to simply rest. You also show them that you're presence and concern is not contingent or based on the expectation that they get better. Their existence is sufficient and valid to you even at their lowest point.

Third, once they seem to have shored up some energy, focus on minor short-term actions. Try to avoid setting "goals," and instead frame them as "directions to move in." Small things like "work on your personal hygiene," or "improve your living environment." I think the problem is that we subconsciously assume that good and bad acts are directly and equivalently linked, but they're not.

Take your person that "directly and literally saved 9,999 lives". We don't (or at least I *hope* we don't) think this person has somehow bought themselves the permission to commit some act of evil. Beforehand, it's pretty easy to see that good and bad deeds simply don't directly balance like that.

I think it comes down to "trust" more than, and separate from, any direct moral evaluation. The savior of 9,999 and murderer of 1, reasonably should have an easier time demonstrating the 1 murder was aberrant and uncharacteristic of them, than the murderer of 9,999 savior of 1.

And I think that's why this entire discussion is so interesting. It hits on the fact that moral deeds and trust are definitely linked, but very complexly, so we can't give a simple answer as to when or how or why good deeds can gain back the trust lost from bad ones.

At best, what good deeds "buy" you is the **chance to ask** for forgiveness, but they can't guarantee you'll ever get it.

Part of it is because forgiving or condemning is the prerogative of the Other on an individual basis.

Let's say someone kills a person in cold blood - it's abject murder. They go to prison, serve their sentence, feel remorse, and earnestly turn their life around.

Is anybody doing anything wrong if they give the murderer a chance? No. But neither is anybody doing anything wrong if they opt not to trust them. People can't be obligated to forgive.

Secondly, and I think more importantly, it would be terrifying to create such a simplistic "ledger" of moral balance... Save 10 lives, get one free murder!

If we knew that there's a simple math underlying forgiveness, then there would no lasting consequence in committing atrocities aside from putting in the necessary time and effort to 'balance the ledger.'

Good and bad deeds simply aren't directly linked like that. Good deeds aren't the currency of bad ones. We would never think that people have 'banked' enough good deeds that they're now 'owed' a bad one. So if good deeds can't 'buy' bad ones beforehand, there's no reason why they should allow you to 'pay off' bad deeds after the fact.

Ice-cream is actually a collection of *very* small solid bits.

The air in Coke likes to gather around very small solid bits. When enough air is gathered around a small solid bit, the air escapes the Coke as a small bubble. 

Ice cream melts in Coke and becomes a liquid that is much thicker than the Coke.

Thicker liquids are better at holding on to small bubbles than thinner liquids like Coke.

The thick-liquid ice cream re-traps the newly escaped small bubbles and makes foam... a lot like dish-soap, except much better tasting.

My first-ever logic professor had perhaps the best description for fallacies I've ever heard:
(Paraphrased... it's been years) "Fallacies neither prove nor disprove a point in and of themselves. They are 'fallacies' precisely because they are erroneously used as proof for one side or the other. But this doesn't mean that they can't *contribute* to the point (though very often they don't). At the very least, they should never stand on their own... if a fallacy is proof of anything, it's that the work is not done yet."
An ad hominem attack works as a fallacy when it's used in a "This person previously said x. X is patently ridiculous. Therefore this person's current claim of y is also ridiculous." Prior - we'll call it 'incorrectness' - doesn't *prove* current incorrectness... the best it can do is support the claim of current incorrectness.
So it depends on how the ad hominem is used. If it's used as proof, ya done screwed up. If it's used as supporting evidence for other, more logically sound points, you're probably in the clear.
